spans.content: THE CHEMICAL COMPOSITION OF THE PASSIVE FILM
ON Fe-24Cr AND Fe-24Cr-11Mo STUDIED BY AES, XPS
AND SIMS
S. MISCHLER, A. VOGEL, H. J. MATHIEU and D. LANDOLT
Materials Department, Swiss Federal Institute of Technology (EPFL), CH-1007 Lausanne, Switzerland
Abstract—A systematic study of the composition and of the thickness of passive films formed at 65°C on
Fe-24Cr and Fe-24Cr-11Mo model alloys in an acid sulfate electrolyte in the presence and absence of
chloride ion at different potentials has been carried out. Non-destructive XPS, AES depth profiling and
dynamic SIMS were applied to the study of the average concentration and the depth distribution of cations
and anions in the films. The apparent film thickness and the average metal ion concentration were found to
be little affected by the presence or absence of chloride ion in the electrolyte. Molybdenum influenced the
depth distribution of chloride ion in the films.
INTRODUCTION
SrAinLEss steels owe their corrosion resistance to the presence of a thin surface oxide
film. The characterization of such films, therefore, is an important field of corrosion
science. Surface analysis methods, in particular AES, XPS and SIMS have been
applied to the study of the chemical composition of passive oxide films on stainless
steels for a number of years and results obtained by different research groups have
been reviewed in the literature. 1.2 It is generally accepted that passive oxide films on
iron-chromium alloys consist predominantly of trivalent chromium oxide.³ Their
thickness is 2–3 nm typically and depends on applied potential.ª The presence in the
films of cations of iron, of molybdenum or of other alloying elements has also been
documented depending on alloy composition.⁵-7 Incorporation of chloride ions has
been observed by some authors but not by others.
Molybdenum is frequently added to ferritic and austenitic stainless steels to
improve their resistance to pitting corrosion in chloride media. It is not known at
present whether passive films on molybdenum containing alloys formed in chloride
media have the same composition as those formed in other media and how they differ
from films on similar alloys not containing molybdenum. Such information could
possibly be of use for the elucidation of pit initiation mechanisms on stainless steels
and the role of molybdenum in this.

EXPERIMENTAL METHOD
The composition of the two alloys used is given in Table 1. The Fe-24Cr–11Mo alloy contained a
higher molybdenum concentration than the usual ferritic stainless steels in order to facilitate analysis of
this element in the passive film. The alloys which are single phase were heat treated at 1300°C for 58 h to
homogenize the elemental concentration. Grain size after heat treatment was in the millimeter range. The
alloys contained a few chromium oxide inclusions.
The electrodes were machined in the form of rods from which rotating disk electrodes were fabricated.
For the determination of polarization curves the disk electrode of 3.57 mm diameter (electrode area
0 . 1 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } )
was embedded in epoxy. For potentiostatic measurements involving surface analysis identical
electrodes were used but without epoxy insulation. By bringing the disk into contact with the electrolyte
surface and slightly pulling back, a meniscus was formed which prevented contact of the side of the rod
with the electrolyte. The rotation rate was 3000 rpm in all experiments.
Two electrolytes were used, 0.1 M
\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 } + 0 . 4 \mathrm { M } \mathrm { N a } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 }
referred to as electrolyte A and 0.1 M
\mathrm { H _ { 2 } S O _ { 4 } } + 0 . 4 \mathrm { M N a _ { 2 } S O _ { 4 } } + 0 . 1 2 \mathrm { M }
NaCl referred to as electrolyte B. All experiments were carried out in
de-aerated solutions under argon. The temperature was
6 5 \mathrm { { ^ \circ C } }
This temperature was chosen because
preliminary experiments had shown that passive films formed at that temperature were slightly thicker
than those formed at
2 5 \mathrm { ‰}
and thus easier to study. At the temperature of the experiments the Fe-Cr alloy
but not the
\mathbf { F e { \mathrm { - } } C r { \mathrm { - } } M o }
alloy exhibited pitting in the electrolyte B.
Electrode pretreatment consisted of mechanical polishing with SiC paper and with 1 μm alumina
powder. The electrodes were washed with ethanol and doubly distilled water before being used.
Polarization curves were determined by applying potential steps and plotting the current measured after
400 s. The measurements were started at a cathodic potential of –650 mV (all potentials in this paper are
given with respect to the normal hydrogen electrode). A potentiostat (Solartron 1286) controlled by a
function generator (AMEL 568) was used. Electrodes used for surface analysis were mechanically
polished and polarized potentiostatically. Three polarization conditions were studied; the condition (CA)
involved cathodic polarization at -650 mV for 1 min. The polarization condition (PL) involved cathodic
polarization at
- 6 5 0 \mathrm { m V }
for 1 min followed by anodic polarization for 1 h at 200 mV. The polarization
condition (PH) was the same as (PL) but anodic polarization was at 500 mV. The current was monitored as
a function of time using an HP 310 computer. At the end of a polarization experiment the electrode was
removed from the electrolyte with the potential still applied, rinsed with doubly distilled water and dried
with argon. It was stored in a desiccator under argon for a maximum of 2 h before being introduced into
the surface analysis apparatus and immediately analysed.

EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
Electrochemical behavior
In Fig. 1 anodic polarization curves of Fe-24Cr and Fe–24Cr–11Mo measured in
electrolytes A and B are given. Pitting in solution B is observed with Fe-24Cr only.
For comparison anodic polarization curves of pure Mo and Cr are shown in Fig. 2.
Transpassive dissolution of Mo starts at close to 0.5 V in both electrolytes, transpas-
sive dissolution of Cr at approximately 1 V. The potential for transpassive dissol-
ution of Cr is of a similar value to that for transpassive dissolution of the non-pitting
alloys in Fig. 1.

The Fe
and the Mo 3d peaks were deconvoluted into a metallic and an
oxidized part without subdividing the latter into different valence states. The average
atomic fraction of the Fe, Cr and Mo cations in the film was calculated using the area
sensitivity factors of Table 3. The results are summarized in Fig. 6. The cathodically
polarized sample (CA) contains significantly more Fe than the anodically polarized
samples (PL) and (PH). Similarly, more molybdenum is present on the cathodically
polarized sample (CA) than on the passivated samples. The concentration of Fe, Cr
and Mo in the metal layers just underneath the film was estimated for the two
alloys,15, but because such data are subject to considerable uncertainty they will not
be discussed here. Indeed, the absolute value of the calculated metal concentration
underneath passive films depends heavily on the procedure used for peak deconvolu-
tion and background subtraction and on the precision of the values of the electron
mean free path employed.

AES depth profiling was used to obtain information on the depth distribution of
different elements and to get additional information on film thickness. Figure 7(a)
shows the AES depth profiles of O, Cr and Fe measured on Fe-24Cr-11Mo polarized
at (PH) in electrolyte B. The profiles shown are corrected for the electron escape
depth.12 The oxygen profile exhibits a well defined oxide-metal interface. Carbon is
present as a surface contamination only, the carbon signal goes to zero at an apparent
depth of approximately 0.3 nm. The Mo signal in the film (Fig. 7b) is weak but
increases at the oxide metal interface. In the alloy it yields an apparent concentration
of 8 at% which is higher than the nominal alloy concentration of 6 at%. The
difference is attributed to Mo enrichment by preferential sputtering of Cr and Fe.16

DISCUSSION
The characterization of passive films by AES, XPS and SIMS is subject to the
limitations inherent in all ex situ methods.¹ An important consideration, therefore, is
to what extent results are affected by the rinsing and sample transfer procedures used
and what reproducibility can be achieved. The former point has been discussed
elsewhere.15,18 Suffice here to mention that SIMS experiments performed with the
^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { O }
isotope indicate that at potentials (PH) the post-oxidation of passive films is
negligible. For the potentials (PL) such experiments are not available but it may be
reasonably supposed that the behavior is similar. The presented data for (PH) and
(PL), therefore, are believed to be representative of the passive film. The (CA) data,
on the other hand, represent the film formed in air during rinsing and transfer and
their reproducibility is limited. It is clear from a comparison of the results that the
chemical composition of the two types of films differs substantially.

their reproducibility is limited. It is clear from a comparison of the results that the
chemical composition of the two types of films differs substantially.
Three parameters were varied in the present study: the potential, alloyed Mo and
the presence of Cl⁻ in the electrolyte. The observed influence of applied potential on
film thickness in the passive region (Fig. 5) and on the Mo content of the films (Fig. 6)
is in qualitative agreement with the literature2,7 although observed differences
between (PL) and (PH) are slight. Alloyed Mo under the present conditions does not
affect the thickness of the passive film in a significant way (Fig. 5), but it alters its
composition because of incorporation of Mo (Fig. 6). The growth-dissolution
behavior of the passive films as revealed by the measured current-time transients
(Fig. 3) is apparently the same in presence and absence of alloyed Mo. This indicates
that at the potentials applied in this study the electrochemical properties of the
passive film are not significantly affected by the molybdenum. In all experiments the
applied potentials were well below the critical pitting potential and no current
instabilities of the type associated in the literature with metastable pitting19 were
observed in this study.
The presence of chloride ion in the electrolyte had little effect on the measured
thickness of the passive films, although the data of Fig. 5 suggest that films formed in
electrolyte B are slightly thinner. The electrolyte composition apparently affects the
distribution of molybdenum in the films; more molybdenum was found in the outer
part of the film formed in electrolyte A than in electrolyte B as is evidenced by the
ratio profiles Mo/Fe + Cr + Mo of Fig. 10.
The XPS, AES and SIMS data suggest that under the conditions of the present
study electrolyte anions are incorporated into the passive films formed on Fe-24Cr
and Fe-24Cr-11Mo. The presence of sulfate is deduced from XPS and AES, the
presence of Cl⁻ from all three methods. The distribution of these species in the film is
not uniform, however, they are concentrated in the outer part of the film. The
thickness of the chloride containing region of the passive films can be estimated from
Fig. 15 taking the 50% value of the maximum amplitude of the Cl⁻ profile as a
measure. One obtains in this way 0.5 nm (PL) and 0.8 nm (PH), respectively for the
Fe-24Cr alloy, 0.4 nm (PL) and 0.7 nm (PH), respectively, for the Fe–24Cr–11Mo
alloy. Since the overall film thickness at a given potential is comparable for the two
alloys it is concluded that Mo affects the chloride ion distribution in the film relatively
more than the overall film thickness. A similar effect of Mo on the sulfur profile at
potential (PH) appears in Fig. 12.
Different interpretations of the observed concentration-depth distribution of
chloride ion, are a priori possible. Firstly, surface analysis methods such as AES,
XPS and SIMS yield average values of concentration over the analysed area which in
the present study is 200 × 200 µm for AES, 700 × 700 μm for SIMS and 3 × 3 mm for
XPS. It cannot be excluded that on a smaller scale the concentration is non-uniform.

For example, if the films contain pores or defects of nanometer size, adsorption of
electrolyte anions at the pore walls could possibly lead to the observation of a

contradiction with the SIMS data of Fig. 14, however. They show only adsorbed
hydroxyl ions but no hydroxide film of a thickness of several atomic layers.

truly incorporated into the passive film where they can occupy positions of oxygen
ions. This poses no conceptual difficulties in the case of chloride ions,20,21 but is more
difficult to visualize for sulfate. The structure of the passive films on the alloys used is
not known but according to McBee and

amorphous. An amorphous structure is expected to facilitate the accommodation of
electrolyte anions but the problem needs further elucidation. If electrolyte anions
are incorporated into the film one may ask why they are located predominantly in the
outer part and why molybdenum affects their depth-distribution. At present no
satisfactory explanation for this behavior is available. According to Takahashi et
al. ,23 who studied anodic films on aluminium in a phosphate electrolyte, the extent of
incorporation of electrolyte anions in the outer part of the barrier film depends on the
transference number of the metal ions in the oxide. Passive films on Fe-Cr and Fe-
Cr-Mo alloys are believed to be n-type semi-conductors.24,25 Another approach,
therefore, might consider the effect of Mo on the space charge in the film.26 Further
studies using in situ experimental techniques will be needed to elucidate these
questions.
CONCLUSIONS
Surface analysis data obtained by AES, XPS and SIMS on passive films formed
under well defined electrochemical conditions in the presence and absence of
chloride ions on two ferritic iron-chromium alloys with and without molybdenum
lead to the following conclusions which are strictly valid for the experimental
conditions of this study.
(1) Alloyed molybdenum has only a minor effect on the thickness of the passive
film and on its growth-dissolution kinetics.
(2) The presence or absence of chloride ion in the electrolyte does not signifi-
cantly change the average metal ion concentration in the film and has only a minor
effect on the film thickness.
(3) Molybdenum and chloride ions rather than being distributed uniformly in the
film are concentrated in its outer part.
(4) Alloyed molybdenum influences the chloride distribution in the film.
